questions.text:
Many coastal towns in New Zealand face increasing risks from sea-level rise and storm surges. Homeowners in these areas bear the cost of flood damage, but the broader costs of coastal development — including emergency services, infrastructure repair, and ecological degradation — are shared by all taxpayers.

Identify and explain the types of market failure present in coastal property development. Use diagrams to illustrate your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: Types of market failure: (1) Negative externality of consumption — each coastal property development imposes costs on the wider community (emergency services, infrastructure protection, environmental damage) that are not reflected in the property price (MSC > MPC). Overdevelopment of coastal land at market prices. (2) Information failure — property buyers may not fully understand the long-term flood and erosion risks. Diagram shows divergence between private and social costs of coastal development.
questions.markingGuide: Identify and explain main categories of market failures relevant to coastal development.

questions.text: Analyse the negative externalities of coastal development in New Zealand, explaining why the free market leads to overdevelopment of at-risk coastal areas. In your answer, distinguish between marginal private cost and marginal social cost of building on the coast.
questions.expectedAnswer: Each developer considers only their private costs (land purchase, construction, insurance). They do not consider the marginal social cost — the additional burden on emergency services, Council infrastructure, and environmental systems. Because MPC < MSC, too many properties are built in at-risk areas (overdevelopment). The deadweight loss represents the net social cost of developments where MSC exceeds the benefit to the owner. As more properties are built, the risk increases non-linearly — each additional property amplifies cumulative demand on shared protective infrastructure.
questions.markingGuide: Show how externalities cause overdevelopment with analysis of MPC vs MSC.

questions.text: The government is considering managed retreat — requiring homeowners in high-risk coastal zones to relocate over a 20-year period. Evaluate the effectiveness of this policy in correcting the market failure. Consider: (1) how the policy addresses the externality, (2) the impact on different groups of homeowners, and (3) how compensation should be structured.
questions.expectedAnswer: Managed retreat corrects the externality by removing the source — no coastal properties means no ongoing costs to taxpayers for flood protection and emergency responses. However, equity concerns arise — homeowners who purchased before risks were understood face forced relocation. Wealthier homeowners may own multiple properties and can absorb the loss, while lower-income homeowners may have their entire wealth in one coastal property. Compensation could be based on current market value, replacement cost, or a declining scale over the 20-year period. The policy is efficient in the long run but socially disruptive.
questions.markingGuide: Critical evaluation of policy options covering efficiency, equity, and compensation design.

questions.text: Compare managed retreat with two alternative policies: (A) building sea walls and flood defences, and (B) requiring mandatory high-risk insurance for all coastal properties. Recommend the best approach for New Zealand, justifying your recommendation with economic analysis.
questions.expectedAnswer: Sea walls: high ongoing cost to taxpayers, creates moral hazard (encourages further coastal development behind the walls), does not address the root externality, and may fail in extreme events. Mandatory insurance: internalises the externality by making coastal property owners pay the true risk cost, discouraging new development through high premiums. But existing owners may become uninsurable, property values collapse, and low-income owners are trapped. Managed retreat: addresses the root cause permanently but is politically difficult and expensive upfront. Recommended approach: mandatory high-risk insurance for existing properties combined with a ban on new development in high-risk zones and a voluntary buyback scheme funded by insurance premiums. This internalises the externality, discourages new development, and provides a pathway out for existing owners.
questions.markingGuide: Sophisticated synthesis comparing three policies and recommending an integrated approach with full justification.
